title: Designing the Perfect Assessment System, Part 1
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Opening a series responding to a UK government review of curriculum and assessment, Daisy Christodoulou returns to the central argument of her 2017 book Making Good Progress: assessment has several distinct, competing purposes, and an assessment designed well for one purpose tends to fail badly at the others. She names four purposes -- summative attainment reporting, formative feedback for improvement, school accountability, and national standards monitoring -- and uses the GCSE as a case study of what happens when one exam is stretched to serve all four, citing the well-documented D/C-borderline intervention-group gaming that resulted. She credits England's post-reform system with partially fixing this by decoupling functions: Progress 8 now carries accountability, the National Reference Test tracks national standards, while GCSE grades remain closer to their original summative purpose. She highlights the National Reference Test and international equivalents like NAEP and PISA as successful examples of decoupled national-standards testing precisely because schools and individuals rarely see their own results, removing the incentive to teach to the test. She closes with a cautionary case study: when England abolished KS2 science national curriculum tests in 2009, schools quickly deprioritised teaching science in favour of tested subjects, showing that removing accountability alongside decoupled sampling can create new problems even as it solves old ones.
points: Christodoulou's four-purpose framework (summative, formative, accountability, national standards) gives a precise diagnostic lens for why a single assessment instrument so often disappoints: it's rarely actually possible to serve all four well at once.

The GCSE case study -- schools building D/C-borderline intervention groups to game grade boundaries -- is concrete historical evidence of what happens when formative, accountability, and national-standards functions all get bolted onto one summative exam.

Her point that decoupled, sampled national tests (NRT, NAEP, PISA) build more trustworthy results specifically because schools rarely see individual outcomes is a structural, not motivational, explanation for measurement validity.

The KS2 science case study is a sharp counter-example showing that decoupling accountability from a subject (not just from an assessment purpose) can itself distort teaching time away from that subject entirely.
quotes: One of the major challenges of designing a good assessment system is that there are a lot of important and competing purposes of assessment.

An assessment that would be perfectly designed for one purpose will not work well for another. Trying to make one assessment fit lots of purposes generally means it ends up fulfilling none of the purposes.
GCSEs were essentially designed to fulfil purpose 1 above. Over time, teachers ended up using them to give feedback and shape the curriculum, the government started using them to judge schools.
This led to lots more students getting the C grade, but the C grade stopped meaning what it had meant previously.
A feature of all these tests is that they are completely decoupled from school accountability and individual attainment.
As soon as 2011, surveys showed that schools had stopped teaching science as much and had reallocated the time to English and maths, which were still being tested.
So the samples have been good at identifying a problem, but can’t provide much information that would help fix it.
